questions.q: What must you do before visualising your data?
options: Make sure it has been cleaned and prepared
Pick the brightest colours available
Publish it online first
Convert it into a pie chart
questions.explain: A chart built on messy data misleads no matter how well it is designed.
questions.evidence: Prior to visualizing your data, you need to ensure that it has been cleaned and prepared

questions.q: One deceptive chart in the lesson reversed its X axis. What did that do?
options: It made the data easier to compare
It hid the chart's title
It changed the colours of the bars
It made the chart show the opposite of the truth
questions.explain: The eye reads left to right, so a reversed date axis suggests cases fell when they rose.
questions.evidence: This chart reverses the X axis to show the opposite of the truth

questions.q: Why can a pie chart with too many categories be a problem?
options: Pie charts cannot show percentages
It uses too little ink
It can be deceptive, even when the intention is good
Pie charts only work for time series
questions.explain: Choosing the wrong type of chart is one of the ways good data gets displayed badly.
questions.evidence: the choice of a bad type of chart, such as a pie chart showing too many categories, can be deceptive

questions.q: What does the 'spurious correlations' website illustrate?
options: Margarine causes divorce
Unrelated things can appear to move together
Correlation always proves causation
Charts should never show two series
questions.explain: It pairs facts like Maine's divorce rate and margarine consumption to show correlation is not causation.
questions.evidence: correlating things like the divorce rate in Maine and the consumption of margarine

questions.q: What test does the guidance suggest for whether a chart is the right choice?
options: If you can't write its message in a few sentences, rethink the chart
If it fits on one slide it is right
If it uses at least three colours it is right
If it has a legend it is right
questions.explain: Imagine describing the chart over the phone: what would you say?
questions.evidence: If you cannot write down the message your chart is giving in a few sentences, you should think again about the chart you have chosen.

questions.q: What should a chart's statistical subtitle say?
options: The author's name and the software used
The main finding in a single word
The colour palette used
What the data is, the geography it covers and the time period shown
questions.explain: The main title gives the message; the statistical subtitle gives the facts behind it.
questions.evidence: The statistical subtitle should say what the data is, the geography the data relates to and the time period shown.

questions.q: Why should values on the y-axis be right aligned?
options: It leaves more room for the legend
It is needed for vertical text
Figures line up units over units and tens over tens, so they are easier to read
It makes the chart look symmetrical
questions.explain: Aligned digits let readers compare magnitudes at a glance.
questions.evidence: When numerical values are right aligned they are easier to read as all the figures are aligned to the right place

questions.q: How should axis labels be written?
options: Diagonally, to save space
Always horizontally
Vertically along the axis
In coloured italic text
questions.explain: Vertical or diagonal text is hard to read; label fewer ticks instead if space is short.
questions.evidence: When labelling axes, always use horizontal text as vertical or diagonal text is hard to read.

questions.q: When are stacked bar charts particularly useful?
options: To compare several part-to-whole relationships in one chart
To show precise values for many categories over time
To display a single headline number
To show how two continuous variables relate
questions.explain: With part-to-whole data every bar has the same length, so the segments are easy to compare.
questions.evidence: Stacked bar charts are particularly useful when you want to compare multiple part-to-whole relationships in one chart.

questions.q: Why does the guidance prefer labelling lines directly instead of using a legend?
options: Legends are banned in official charts
Direct labels make the lines thicker
Legends always cover part of the data
A legend makes users match labels to lines by colour
questions.explain: Matching by colour is hard for many users, especially with several lines.
questions.evidence: This is better than using a legend which relies on users matching labels to lines using colour.

questions.q: If you show several small line charts side by side, what is essential?
options: Each chart uses a different colour
Each chart has its own legend
All the y-axes have the same scale
Every x-axis starts at zero
questions.explain: Different scales make similar-looking lines mean very different things.
questions.evidence: If you use these, it is essential for all the y-axes to have the same scale to avoid misunderstandings.

questions.q: How should the categories in a pie chart be ordered?
options: Alphabetically, starting at 3 o'clock
Ranked by size, with the first sector starting at 12 o'clock
Randomly, so no category dominates
Smallest first, starting at 6 o'clock
questions.explain: Label the sectors directly rather than using a key.
questions.evidence: Rank the categories in a pie chart by size and start the first sector at the 12

questions.q: What does the accessibility standard require for all non-text content such as charts?
options: A text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose
At least three different colours
A downloadable spreadsheet
A printed copy on request
questions.explain: So every data visualisation needs alternative text that communicates its message.
questions.evidence: All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

questions.q: What does the guidance note about people with mild colour blindness?
options: They cannot see blue at all
They see every colour as grey
They can read any palette without help
They may see a colour only if there is enough of it
questions.explain: Thin lines or small areas of colour can be invisible to them, so colour should never be the only cue.
questions.evidence: are able to see a colour, but only if there is enough

questions.q: Which colours does the guidance recommend for sequential data?
options: As many contrasting hues as possible
Red for low values and green for high values
A single hue, or a small set of closely related hues
Black and white only
questions.explain: Sequential palettes should still be used only when necessary, alongside other cues.
questions.evidence: When you are presenting sequential data, it is best to use a single hue, or small set of closely related hues.

questions.q: How do demonstration tables differ from reference tables?
options: Demonstration tables are interactive; reference tables are printed
Demonstration tables back up a point in the text; reference tables supply reusable data
Demonstration tables are for experts; reference tables for the public
They are the same thing
questions.explain: Keep demonstration tables small and focused; reference tables can be large.
questions.evidence: Demonstration tables are used to reinforce a point made in the text of a publication.

questions.q: How should the data columns of a table be formatted?
options: Right aligned, with the same precision within each column
Centred, with varying decimal places
Left aligned and rounded to whole numbers
Every value in bold
questions.explain: Consistent precision and alignment make values easy to compare down a column.
questions.evidence: The data columns are right aligned and the same level of precision is used within each column

questions.q: Why should images of tables never be used in publications?
options: They take too long to print
They cannot be resized
They are blocked on mobile phones
They fail the accessibility criterion on images of text
questions.explain: Publish tables as marked-up HTML so screen readers can navigate rows and columns.
questions.evidence: Images of tables should never be used as they fail accessibility success criterion 1.4.5 images of text
